Veteran investor Peter Schiff claimed Google parent Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Gemini AI gave him answers that challenged the official account of the investigation into his former bank.

Schiff, who founded Euro Pacific International Bank, has long disputed the circumstances surrounding its closure following scrutiny by the IRS and OCIF as part of the J5 investigation.

Schiff Claims Gemini AI Challenges Bank Probe Findings

On Saturday, Schiff said on X that questioning Google’s AI-powered search responses could lead Gemini to conclude that a bank did nothing wrong.

"What is interesting is that in AI mode, if you question Google’s response, Gemini will explain the initial search results and conclude on its own that the evidence actually shows the bank did nothing wrong," Schiff wrote.

He alleged that the IRS, Australian Taxation Office (ATO) and OCIF "lied to save face" after a highly publicized investigation allegedly failed to uncover wrongdoing.

Schiff also accused the media of reporting the government’s version of events instead of the truth.

He wrote that outlets reported "what the governments wanted the public to believe, rather than the truth," and urged users to test Gemini’s responses themselves, adding, "Try it for yourself."

Google Expanded Gemini’s Reach and AI Ambitions

In August, Google announced that Gemini had reached 1 billion monthly active users, with 63% preferring voice interactions and its image-generation tool producing about 150 million images daily.

Sundar Pichai called it Google’s 14th product to reach the milestone and its fastest-growing ever.

In July, Pichai said Google had begun its "most ambitious pretraining run yet" for Gemini 4, targeting future AI capabilities without announcing a launch date.

He also highlighted coding improvements in Gemini Flash 3.6 and plans to release updated models monthly amid intensifying competition.

Last year, Google unveiled Gemini 3, describing it as its most capable and nuanced AI system, with improved multimodal and agentic capabilities to compete with OpenAI’s GPT-5.

AI Search Competition Intensified

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) launched AI-powered Facebook Search using its Muse Spark model, a move an analyst said could generate billions of dollars in annual revenue.

Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo reported a 30% week-over-week surge in U.S. installs amid criticism of Google’s AI search features, urging users to switch platforms. Google still held about 90% of the global search market in April 2026.

news.content:
U.S. corporate profits hit a record $4.7 trillion in the 12 months through mid-year, up 17%. Meanwhile, just 42 AI-related companies accounted for around two-thirds of the S&P 500’s gains since early 2024, according to WNYC.

Bulls call it an AI revolution. BCA Research’s Peter Berezin and Minack Advisors’ Gerard Minack see an accounting asymmetry instead.

“Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) earns a big profit whenever it sells a GPU,” Berezin wrote.

“Whoever buys that chip, however, does not incur an immediate cost because the purchase is treated as capital spending.” Buyers depreciate the chips over roughly six years, while Nvidia books the full sale upfront. Cash flows don’t change, but reported earnings rise.

“This is probably the most earnings accretive capex boom in history,” Jefferies strategist Christopher Wood noted, according to Reuters.

The $1 Trillion Capex Mirage

Depreciation doesn’t start until a data center comes online. Morgan Stanley estimates that as much as 40% of this year’s AI capex won’t be operational until 2027–2029. By decade’s end, hyperscalers’ annual depreciation charges will run between $500 billion and $1 trillion, according to Capital Gearing Asset Management.

Paper gains add a second boost. Tech giants book changes in the value of their stakes in unlisted labs like OpenAI and Anthropic as “other non-operating income.” In the four quarters to mid-2026, annualized earnings at Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) rose by $222 billion.

Over the same period, that non-operating line rose by $224 billion, which accounts for all of their reported profit growth.

Minsky’s ‘Ponzi Finance’ Hits the Neoclouds

This year the hyperscalers are putting almost all of their operating cash flow into capex. They’ve issued about $225 billion of unsecured bonds, roughly 30% of full-year capital spending. They also hold $1.1 trillion in lease commitments that stay off their balance sheets.

Morgan Stanley forecasts the group will have negative free cash flow of about $550 billion next year.

Economist Hyman Minsky used the term “Ponzi finance” for businesses that can’t cover their outgoings from cash flow and rely on rising valuations to raise capital. Loss-making data center operators and frontier labs fit that description.

The ‘Profits Bubble’ Trap

Tech stocks don’t look expensive relative to earnings. “The bubble is in profits, not valuations,” financial historian Edward Chancellor argued for Reuters Breakingviews. U.S. homebuilders were in the same position in 2006, and global miners were in the same position when the commodity supercycle stalled in the mid-2010s.

He points to Minack’s warning that, when the capex boom ends, earnings growth could revert to trend. Tighter credit could make the $550 billion cash shortfall hard to fund. Falling valuations for neoclouds and private labs would reverse the paper gains, and the 2027–2030 depreciation wall would start hitting income statements.

The irony, as WNYC notes, is that fierce price competition among AI labs could crush tech margins. The same competition could make automation cheap enough for cash-strapped firms to cut white-collar jobs in the downturn that follows.
news.headline: A $1 Trillion Depreciation Bomb Is Ticking Beneath the AI Market
news.summary: Wall Street’s record profit boom looks less like a productivity miracle and more like an accounting mirage, and the bill comes due by 2030.

AI Stock Bubble Index Has Hit 74

There are signs that we are in an AI bubble. The AI Stock Bubble Index has trended steadily higher this year and now stands in the extreme zone at 74. This reading suggests that infrastructure spending and valuations are running ahead of disclosed revenue.

The index’s rise has happened at a time when some analysts are warning of the bubble. Ray Dalio has warned that it may burst because of rising interest rates, while Ken Griffin compared it to the dot-com bubble. 

Neocloud companies like CoreWeave, IREN, Nebius, and The RUM Group are at a significant risk if the bubble bursts. In a recent note, Gartner (NYSE:IT) said that these companies are at a bigger risk than hyperscalers. It warned that over $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to impairment by the end of 2030.

These fears explain why CoreWeave’s stock has tumbled, and its short interest has risen to 15%. Its bond yields have also kept climbing, with the notes maturing in 2031 now yielding 15%. Total debt has jumped to nearly $30 billion, and capital expenditure is expected to remain substantially high.

Another risk is that the neocloud industry is being highly competitive. Virtually all Bitcoin mining companies have expanded into the sector. RUM Group (NASDAQ:RUM), formerly known as Rumble, has expanded into the industry by buying Northern Data. 

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) has received orders from companies like Google and Anthropic. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) has also expanded to the industry, while many private companies like Lambda, Nscale, and Firmus are gaining market share. 

CoreWeave Stock is at Risk of Falling Below $50

The daily chart shows that the CRWV shares have continued falling in the past few months. It has dropped below the important support level of $64, which was the neckline of the head-and-shoulders pattern. 

The stock has dropped below the 50-day moving average and the Strong, Pivot reverse of the Murrey Math Lines tool at $75. It has remained below the Supertrend indicator. 

Therefore, the stock will likely continue falling, potentially to Murrey Math Lines’ Ultimate Support level of $50. A drop below that level will point to more downside towards the oversold level of $37.5.

Broader AI Bubble Warning

Apollo Global Management Inc.‘s chief economist, Torsten Slok, said AI has produced substantial financial benefits mainly for large technology companies, while its broader impact across corporate America remains difficult to detect.

Slok published his analysis on Saturday, examining AI’s economic effects across sectors. He compared the Magnificent Seven stocks, which include Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA), with the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.

He found that technology companies’ revenue per employee increased from roughly $550,000 in 2022 to almost $800,000. The figure stayed near $550,000 for the remaining S&P 500 companies during the same period.

“The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector,” Slok wrote.

Technology profit margins also widened after 2022, while margins for other companies remained close to 10%. Apollo said it found no significant economywide productivity increase attributable to AI. Slok also said AI has yet to deliver the major productivity gains optimists predicted.

"Despite massive investments and widespread hype about artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok said.

The Apollo chief economist said mainstream companies increasingly treat AI spending as a cost center that pressures margins, while questioning whether lower-cost tools can eventually generate stronger revenue growth and profitability. “That may be harder than it sounds,” he said.

Read Also: The AI Boom Isn't 1999—and Big Tech Could Cushion a Market Crash, This CEO Says

AI Boom Raises Crowding-Out Concerns

The findings arrive amid broader concerns that AI investment is concentrating economic gains while diverting capital from other priorities. Earlier this month, economist Paul Krugman said that the AI boom poses an immediate economic risk by driving up interest rates and crowding out other investments. He says data center construction is diverting capital from housing, offices and factories, a trend visible in FRED data since early 2023.

A previous analysis by JPMorgan warned that the U.S. economy and stock market are increasingly dependent on AI, with 42 AI-related stocks driving 60% to 80% of S&P 500 earnings growth, price returns and capital spending since January 2024.

Meanwhile, 60% of S&P 500 stocks are down at least 20% from their highs, only 30% are outperforming the index, AI gains are concentrated among suppliers rather than adopters, technology’s contribution to GDP growth has risen to about 33%, and only 20% of states are growing faster than the national average.

On the other hand, veteran technology investor Paul Wick has drawn parallels between today’s AI surge and the dot-com era, while saying today’s AI boom differs from the dot-com bubble because IPO activity and dramatic first-day stock surges remain muted, while enterprise AI spending and recent tech earnings remain resilient.

Analyst Warns Delays Could Destroy Neoclouds

Market commentator Nicholas Mugalli warned that rising penalties for delayed data centers could threaten heavily indebted neocloud operators, even as demand for AI computing remains strong.

"$5M/day late penalties prove two things that @elonmusk has been talking about when it comes to Neoclouds," Mugalli wrote Monday on X.

"Extremely bullish for demand. The ROI on active compute is so high that downtime is an existential threat," he explained, citing reports that customers now demand penalties exceeding $5 million daily for delayed facilities, compared with approximately $1 million previously.

Mugalli estimated construction and equipment costs at $57 million per megawatt, including $37.5 million for servers.

"Huge tailwind for power and cooling infrastructure. Death sentence for slow developers," he warned.

Musk Predicts Widespread Neocloud Industry Shakeout

Mugalli’s comments follow Musk’s warning about the tightening neocloud financing market.

Musk said debt markets had "almost entirely shut off access to money" for companies lacking substantial revenue outside AI data centers. He predicted "guppy-level death and consolidation" among more than 200 neocloud providers.

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) on Sunday secured $40 billion in financing for Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) GPUs, highlighting the industry’s enormous capital requirements.

Financing Pressures Mount Despite Strong Demand

JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM) CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that artificial intelligence agents accessing customer accounts pose serious security risks, but AI researcher Andrew Yoon argued banks may have another reason to resist the technology: the potential threat to their profits.

Dimon Warns AI Agents Could Threaten Banks

Speaking on NewsNation’s Morning in America, Yoon, head of research at Civ AI, said autonomous agents could help customers transfer idle cash into higher-yield savings accounts.

"For a consumer, this is good for you. You save money," Yoon said. "But for a bank, if millions of their customers are doing this, they’re actually seeing a pretty significant threat to their bottom line."

Dimon previously warned that AI agents could act against customers’ interests, particularly when users provide banking credentials.

"You’re assuming they’re gonna act properly on your behalf, and they may not," he said during an October 14 Economic Club of Chicago appearance, adding that agents could do things "treacherous for the bank, too."

Reuters reported Thursday that JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS), Bank of America Corporation (NYSE:BAC) and other major lenders were restricting third-party AI agents amid concerns about agents accessing accounts and potentially taking actions independent of users’ instructions.

Read Also: Sundar Pichai Is Using AI Agents to Track Google 24/7: 'Made All of Us… Be Better at What We Do'

AI Agents Could Threaten Banking Profits

Yoon questioned whether banks should decide which financial tools customers can use, arguing that account holders may authorize agents independently.

"If I, as a consumer, want to use a tool to access my financial systems, maybe that should be up to me," he said, while acknowledging risks from malicious instructions that manipulate agents.

McKinsey estimated in April 2026 that automated transfers of just 5% to 10% of checking balances into higher-yield accounts could reduce banks’ deposit profits by at least 20%. Its research also warns that AI agents could weaken banks’ direct customer relationships.

Banks Face Growing Pressure From AI

The concerns follow warnings from lawmakers about rogue financial AI agents, as financial institutions seek stronger controls over automated transactions.

Meanwhile, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) Muse is expanding AI-powered commerce, raising questions about who controls customer relationships.

Yoon acknowledged that attackers could exploit prompt-injection vulnerabilities to manipulate agents into unauthorized transactions. Banks, however, maintain that their restrictions primarily protect customers against security breaches and unintended financial activity.

The Path to $150 Crude

During a recent podcast interview with Mario Nafwal, El-Erian stated that if a broader war breaks out and disrupts tanker flows in the Straits and the Red Sea, prices will climb significantly. “This is not oil at 120. This is oil at 150 because we don’t have these two other things that we had before,” El-Erian said.

He explained that the market previously avoided $150 oil because China cut its imports by 40% and relied heavily on both sovereign and company inventories. With those global inventories now drawn down, El-Erian stated that the market lacks its prior buffers.

Trump Rules Out Immediate Strike

El-Erian’s warning comes amid short-term market relief following recent comments from President Trump. Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Sunday, Oct. 25, Trump stated that the U.S. would not immediately attack Iran.

“The answer is no,” Trump said. “There will not be a strike today.”

Following Trump’s remarks, oil prices retreated. However, tensions remain high, as U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have tightened security due to intelligence warnings of Iranian plots, and the Pentagon has reportedly prepared options for follow-up strikes.

Economic Tipping Points

Despite the immediate drop in oil prices, El-Erian cautioned that a prolonged conflict would serve as a “major headwind” for the global economy, particularly as borrowing costs remain elevated.

El-Erian noted that recent market stability has been built on “borrowed resilience,” as nations drew down existing inventories and financial wealth. “You can’t keep on borrowing from inventories all the time,” El-Erian stated.

If these buffers fail during a prolonged military conflict, El-Erian concluded that the resulting energy shock would deliver a “significant blow” to the global economy and “undermine the marketplace.”

CrowdStrike and Nvidia Expanded AI Agent Security From Software to Silicon

On Oct. 21, at Nvidia’s GTC conference, CrowdStrike announced an expanded collaboration with Nvidia to extend AI-native security from software to hardware. CrowdStrike is integrating Falcon Guardian, its AI Detection and Response product, with Nvidia’s OpenShell secure runtime software, and plans to integrate it with Nvidia Sentry for in-silicon enforcement. The OpenShell integration will connect agent prompts, model interactions and runtime activity with the broader Falcon platform’s security context, to help enterprises detect malicious behavior across AI agent workflows.

The planned Sentry integration, on Nvidia’s BlueField-4 data processing units, would pair AI detection and response with out-of-band monitoring and hardware-level policy enforcement, to contain unsafe agent behavior beyond the software runtime.

"AI agents have already created a new attack surface, and guardrails alone won’t stop an adversary," said Daniel Bernard, chief business officer at CrowdStrike.

An Apollo-managed entity would buy equipment, including Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) chips, and lease it to SpaceX for about five years. The interest rate remains undetermined, and closing is expected by year-end.

SpaceX’s Expensive AI Expansion

SpaceX’s Super Intelligence division, including Grok and cloud computing services, generated $7.56 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 830% year over year.

However, its quarterly capital spending hit $16.44 billion, more than twice revenue. The division reported a $431 million operating profit.

The separate leasing structure is intended to keep borrowing off SpaceX’s balance sheet and protect its investment-grade rating, Bloomberg reported. The eventual accounting treatment remains uncertain.

AI Debt Markets Under Pressure

The most expensive portion of the financing could cost up to 8.75%, Semafor reported Monday, compared with 6.65% on SpaceX’s priciest bonds issued in June. The instruments differ, but the figures underscore rising financing costs.

CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) has also come under pressure. Its bonds issued in June at a 9.675% yield were yielding roughly 15% by mid-October, Reuters reported.

Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas estimates SpaceX could issue another $230 billion in debt between 2027 and 2029 to finance its expansion.

“This is the biggest risk to our model, and we do not want to downplay it,” Jonas wrote, warning that difficulty raising the money could undermine his forecasts for SpaceX’s growth.

Musk Warns of a Neocloud Shakeout

Musk warned in his Sunday X post that debt markets had “almost entirely shut off access to money” for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

He predicted “guppy-level death and consolidation” among what he said were more than 200 neocloud providers, companies renting computing power to AI developers.

Musk argues Starlink and launch revenues give SpaceX an advantage. It ended September with nearly $90 billion in cash and marketable securities against roughly $39 billion in debt and finance leases.

On Polymarket, traders put the odds of a qualifying AI downturn by December 31 at roughly 10%. The contract requires three specified distress events within 90 days.

Apollo and Blackstone announced a $35 billion deal to finance chips for Anthropic in June, part of an AI lending boom that could reach $1 trillion, as Benzinga reported last week.

The platform will debut at Dangote Petroleum Refinery in Lekki, Nigeria, where Honeywell estimates it could generate more than $60 million in gross annual operational benefits at full capacity.

Honeywell Targets $60 Million-Plus Benefit At Dangote Refinery

Forge Plant Cognition combines operating data, engineering expertise and physics-based models to identify bottlenecks, anticipate problems and recommend actions.

Honeywell estimates AI-enabled optimization at the Dangote refinery could deliver more than 29 cents per barrel in operational benefits, excluding implementation costs.

The platform uses Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA technologies to support plant optimization, digital twins, anomaly detection and simulation-based planning.

Dangote will combine refinery data with Honeywell’s AI and process expertise to improve troubleshooting, decision-making and plant performance.

The platform will also support Dangote’s goal of developing a 70% Nigerian workforce by expanding access to specialized process knowledge.

"By collaborating with Dangote to launch Forge Plant Cognition, we are demonstrating how AI can help transform industrial operations, driving new levels of productivity, reliability and profitability at significant scale," said Rajesh Gattupalli, President, Honeywell Technologies UOP.

Q3 Results Add Financial Context

The AI launch follows Honeywell’s third-quarter results, when adjusted EPS of $2.27 topped the $2.17 estimate. Revenue rose 1% year over year to $4.994 billion but missed the $5.007 billion consensus.

Organic sales increased 7%, while short-cycle organic orders rose 8%, excluding businesses divested during the quarter.

In April 2015, Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) was a $12 billion maker of graphics cards for video gamers.

Today, it is worth more than $5 trillion and powers the artificial intelligence boom.

Yet, Nvidia’s stock has just hit its biggest discount to the market since then.

Wall Street expects Nvidia to earn $12.03 per share over the next 12 months. At the end of 2022, that estimate was roughly 40 cents.

At around $215, the stock trades at about 18 times those expected earnings. The S&P 500, tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), trades at 19 times.

So why is the market paying less for a company that keeps earning more?

Nvidia weekly chart, next-12-month EPS estimate and forward P/E ratio. Source: TradingView

Nvidia Stock Trades at an 11% Discount to the Market

When OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, Nvidia traded at more than 40 times forward earnings.

Since then, profits have risen far faster than the share price.

As a result, the multiple fell to 18 at Friday’s close, less than half its 2022 level and near the lowest reading in eight years.

The comparison with the broader market is even more striking.

At Friday’s close, Nvidia traded at an 11% discount to the average company in the S&P 500. The gap had not been this wide since April 2015, when the company’s biggest customers were still gamers rather than hyperscalers.

Two Fears Are Weighing on Nvidia Stock

The first concern is how long its biggest customers can keep spending.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) are on track to invest $930 billion this year. Estimates point to $1.35 trillion next year.

After that, however, the curve flattens. Projections show $1.45 trillion the following year and $1.415 trillion the year after.

For this reason, if spending stops growing, Nvidia’s growth faces the same ceiling.

Read Also: Meta Just Burned Cash for the First Time Since Its IPO Year: Wall Street Raised Its Targets Anyway

The second fear is the neoclouds.

Companies such as CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) and Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) borrow money to buy Nvidia chips, then rent that computing power to AI developers.

The model works as long as demand stays high and money stays cheap. Lately, both conditions are being tested.

Investors now demand more than 16% to lend to CoreWeave, and its shares have lost 42% over the past month. Nebius is down 38% over the same stretch, and both fell more than 3% in early trading Monday.

Even Jensen Huang acknowledged the problem on Oct. 22, saying demand for computing far exceeds the capital available to finance it. Nvidia fell 4.4% that day.

The financing question resurfaced Monday. Meta, which plans a $95 billion funding push for its AI ambitions, said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) had each indicated interest in buying up to $5 billion of shares in its stock offering.

In other words, the chipmakers are now helping fund one of their biggest customers.

Read Also: CoreWeave Bonds Stop Bleeding After SpaceX Results, But Investors Still Demand 3x Treasury Yields

Wall Street Still Sees the Discount as an Opportunity

Analysts, however, are not backing away.

Nvidia has a consensus Buy rating from the 29 analysts tracked by Benzinga Analyst Ratings. Their average price target of $343 implies about 59% upside. Over the past three months, targets have ranged from $300 to $515, the high end set by Raymond James.

The most recent call came on Oct. 22, when Needham analyst N. Quinn Bolton maintained a Buy rating and a $300 target.

Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse reiterated an Overweight rating and a $350 target after attending Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote.

Muse said Nvidia’s guidance for more than 70% revenue growth in calendar 2027 looks very conservative.

He highlighted demand that still supports well above 100% growth, and supply deals that should expand Nvidia’s substrate capacity 2.5 times over three years.

With shares trading at less than 10 times Cantor’s calendar 2028 earnings estimate, the stock is “simply too hard to ignore,” Muse said.

The Market Has Doubted Nvidia Before

In 2015, investors priced Nvidia as a gaming company with limited prospects. That discount turned out to be one of the great mispricings in market history.

Today, they are pricing the world’s main AI supplier as if its growth is about to stall.

Whether that doubt proves equally misplaced no longer depends on demand for Nvidia’s chips. It depends on whether its customers can keep paying for them.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) plans to raise about $95 billion for its artificial intelligence expansion, with three of its biggest chip suppliers considering buying shares in their own customer.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) have expressed interest in purchasing up to $5 billion of Meta’s Class A shares collectively, the company announced Monday.

The potential investments are nonbinding.

Meta launched approximately $35 billion in offerings, comprising $22.5 billion of common stock and $12.5 billion in securities convertible into shares. It will receive proceeds from the common-stock portion when forward-sale agreements settle, rather than immediately.

The company also plans another $60 billion in share sales beginning in early 2027, although that program is not guaranteed.

The Financial Times reported that Alphabet and SpaceX have also turned to equity markets to fund their expansion, with Anthropic preparing to follow.

Chip Suppliers Could Become Shareholders

Meta is already a major customer of all three companies. Nvidia has agreed to supply millions of AI chips, AMD has a deal covering up to six gigawatts of GPUs, and Broadcom is helping develop Meta’s custom processors.

Investing in Meta would give the chipmakers another way to benefit from its AI expansion, not just as suppliers but as shareholders.

The relationship with AMD is particularly interesting. In February, AMD granted Meta warrants to buy up to 160 million AMD shares for one cent each, subject to chip purchases and other performance milestones.

If AMD proceeds with its proposed investment, the two companies could end up owning stakes in each other.

AI Spending Squeezes Cash Flow

Meta expects capital spending of $135 billion to $145 billion this year.

Despite third-quarter revenue climbing 26% to $64.6 billion, the company recorded negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion as infrastructure spending outpaced operating cash generation.

“Our investments are paying off,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last week, pointing to progress in Meta’s core business.

The increasingly close financial relationships between AI suppliers and customers have nevertheless attracted scrutiny.

In an analysis published last Wednesday, LSEG researchers David McNay and Robin Marshall warned that, across the wider industry, “ownership webs can make tracking the revenue to earnings a forensic accounting exercise.”

They argued that such arrangements can make it harder to identify where independent demand originates and who ultimately bears the financial risks.

AI Bubble Odds

On Polymarket, traders put the probability of a qualifying AI industry downturn at 10% by December 31, 2026, rising to 23% by June 30, 2027.

The December contract has attracted approximately $2.5 million in trading volume, compared with just $38,000 for the June market.

The contract requires three specified distress events within 90 days, including sharp declines in semiconductor stocks or the bankruptcy of a major AI developer.

Meta’s planned $60 billion program would use its new nonvoting shares, allowing it to raise capital without diluting Zuckerberg’s voting control.

ERShares founder and chief investment officer Joel Shulman said ERShares Private-Public Crossover ETF‘s (NASDAQ:XOVR) maintains approximately 18%–20% exposure to SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), making any M&A activity involving the rocket manufacturer particularly significant for the fund.

“We are extremely bullish on SpaceX as a standalone investment and view it as a multidecade holding, much like our investment in Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) over the past 21 years,” Shulman told Benzinga.

However, his optimism about SpaceX comes with a key concern: the price it might pay to acquire Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA).

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: A SpaceX–Tesla Merger Could Boost Passive ETF Demand, But ERShares’ Joel Shulman Flags a Big Risk

“My greatest concern is the price SpaceX would have to pay to acquire Tesla,” Shulman added. “Tesla already trades at historically elevated valuation multiples, and its shareholders would likely demand an additional acquisition premium.”

For XOVR, the transaction’s implications would depend on the valuation assigned to both businesses and the consideration received for SpaceX shares. If SpaceX pays a substantial premium, existing SpaceX shareholders could surrender some of their potential long-term gains to Tesla shareholders.

A stock-for-stock transaction could also dilute existing SpaceX shareholders by increasing the combined company’s share count.

“Preserving [Elon] Musk’s control while protecting shareholder value would be central to the transaction structure,” Shulman said, identifying free cash flow per share and long-term earnings growth as key measures of success.

How Could a Merger Affect XOVR?

XOVR does not directly hold SpaceX shares. According to ERShares’ disclosures, it gains exposure indirectly through special purpose vehicles (SPVs) linked to private-market securities. The fund’s reported SpaceX SPV position represented 18.28% of net assets.

The transaction’s impact would depend on its structure, including whether the SPV receives shares in the combined company, cash or other consideration. The resulting valuation and market reaction would also affect the fund’s reported exposure and net asset value.

Shulman said, “The ultimate impact on XOVR would depend on the transaction valuation, exchange ratio and market reaction.”

A merger could create opportunities across artificial intelligence, robotics, autonomous driving and satellite communications. However, Shulman cautioned that technological synergies could take years to translate into measurable earnings.

What Investors Should Watch

For XOVR shareholders, the central question is whether a merger enhances SpaceX’s long-term value or diverts resources toward an expensive acquisition.

Investors should monitor the proposed exchange ratio, any acquisition premium, potential dilution and the combined company’s ability to generate free cash flow per share.

No deal terms have been agreed, and both companies’ boards are evaluating a potential combination. SpaceX’s SEC filing states that no assurance exists that a transaction will be reached or completed.

For XOVR, the outcome could ultimately depend less on the headline size of a combined Musk-led enterprise and more on how much value SpaceX shareholders retain after the deal.

Anthropic PBC grew revenue to $16.29 billion in the six months ended June 30, up from $1.16 billion in the same period a year earlier, according to the company’s S-1 registration statement filed with the SEC on Monday.

The numbers trace one of the steepest revenue climbs on record. Anthropic recorded $41 million in sales in 2023, the year Claude launched commercially. Revenue reached $386 million in 2024 and $4.59 billion in 2025. The first half of 2026 alone produced more than three times the prior full-year total.

The San Francisco-based AI developer has applied to list its Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT. 

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead the underwriting group with units of JPMorgan Chase and Citigroup also appearing on the deal.

Read Also: Anthropic Publicly Files for IPO: What Will ANT Stock Be Worth on Day One?

Big Tech Has a Stake

Several of the largest stocks in the market are tied to Anthropic’s growth. Claude is sold through Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, the cloud platforms run by Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) and Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT). Anthropic pays each provider a fee under a joint go-to-market arrangement, the filing says.

Spending climbed too. Compute and infrastructure expenses hit $8.95 billion in the first half, compared with $2.33 billion a year earlier. Even so, Anthropic said second-quarter revenue grew 1,368% year over year while compute costs rose 300%.

Read Also: Anthropic Has Over $600 Billion in Compute Contracts — And It's Not Enough

The company trains and runs its models on a mix of hardware, including Amazon’s Trainium chips, Google’s TPUs and graphics processors from NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD). 

Amazon Web Services also holds convertible notes, a portion of which will convert into Anthropic stock before the offering is completed, subject to an ownership cap

Losses Look Huge on Paper

Anthropic posted a net loss of $80.75 billion for the six months. Most of it came from a $72.39 billion charge tied to changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs, which the company attributed mainly to its rising valuation.

The operating loss narrowed to $693 million from $2.14 billion. On an adjusted basis, Anthropic reported operating income of $1.62 billion and a 10% adjusted operating margin.

The balance sheet is deep. Anthropic held $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents plus $19.3 billion in short-term investments as of June 30, after raising $141.1 billion in total capital.

Customer data helps explain the surge. As of Sept. 30, more than 11,900 customers had generated at least $100,000 in trailing 12-month revenue, and about 250 had topped $10 million. Net revenue retention stood near 900%.

An Unusual Ownership Setup

Public shareholders will have limited control. A Long-Term Benefit Trust will elect a majority of the board, and an entity owned by the seven co-founders will hold 50.1% of total voting power on general matters.

Share count and price range have not been disclosed.

news.content:
Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) ended its agreement to anchor Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA)-backed Nscale’s proposed 50-megawatt artificial intelligence data center in Loughton, Essex, after the expected grid connection slipped into the 2030s.

Over 23,000 Nvidia chips were set to power the site starting in 2027, providing computing power for Microsoft’s Azure cloud business. Although Microsoft stressed that the implications affect only this site, not the broader partnership with Nscale, they extend beyond a single facility.

"Preferences are optional and subject to constraints, whereas constraints are neither optional nor subject to preferences," BCA Research’s Marko Papić stated in his book "The Geopolitical Alpha."

For Microsoft, picking Loughton was an operational preference. But the physical grid connection is an unyielding constraint. Even the world’s most cash-rich software company cannot flip the switch on an AI supercluster before the electricity arrives, exposing the hard limits of capital expenditure against sluggish utility infrastructure. 

Superfactory Ambitions Against Physical Limitations

The financial stakes are sizeable. Microsoft’s 2026 annual report disclosed $34.6 billion committed to construction and improvements, mainly data centers. The report also acknowledged that those facilities depend on reliable energy and suitable land.

CEO Satya Nadella described a record fiscal 2026, with Azure growing 41% and surpassing $100 billion for the first time.

Microsoft added 88 new data centers during the year, including what Nadella called a “first-of-its-kind superfactory” spanning its Fairwater sites in Atlanta and Wisconsin.

Nadella praised the firm’s performance and utilization per dollar and per watt, calling them the "cost-to-outcome" frontier.

The company’s custom Maia 300 chip “delivers 40 percent more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” he said. Still, gains from in-house hardware can’t make utilities shorten grid-connection queues that run for years.

‘Announced Is Not Executable’

The Loughton example is the textbook constraint outlined in a Quilter Cheviot report, where Ben Barringer, the firm’s global head of technology research, pointed to power, grid, permits, land and labor as constraints that are “slowing down the potential usage of AI technology.”

Money isn’t the shortage. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle are expected to spend $4.2 trillion in the four years ending 2029, according to analyst estimates on FactSet.

The firm also forecasts AI capital spending will reach $1.2 trillion in 2027, with about 20% expected to be financed by debt. Even so, capital alone can’t clear infrastructure bottlenecks.

“Announced capacity is not the same as executable capacity,” Janus Henderson wrote. The firm cited more than 120 U.S. data-center projects worth about $200 billion that were reportedly blocked or delayed in the first half of 2026.

Social License and Time-to-Revenue Risk

Community opposition over electricity prices, water use, and noise is also changing project timelines. Janus Henderson notes over 300 temporary or permanent bans passed at U.S. state and local levels since 2023.

Delayed projects aren’t necessarily canceled for good, and Microsoft’s wider expansion hasn’t stalled. But as Quilter Cheviot noted, hyperscalers can only monetize a data center “once it is completed and switched on.” Billions can pay for buildings and processors without guaranteeing when they’ll start earning revenue.

“The likely winners in the AI capacity race will not simply be those announcing the most ambitious buildouts,” Janus Henderson wrote. 

The winners will be the companies that can secure reliable power and still keep community support. In other words, the ones that can actually plug in.

news.content:
AI agents are being designed to do more than answer questions: They can access files, use workplace tools and carry out tasks with less human supervision. But giving software that much freedom creates a new risk. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) wants to make these digital assistants safer to use, though BNP Paribas analyst Karl Ackerman sees a potential trade-off: runtime could slow by as much as 25%.

Giving AI More Freedom—With Limits

Nvidia announced its OpenShell reference architecture at GTC Berlin recently, building on open-source software designed to control what AI agents can access and do. The system is intended to set boundaries around agents as they work, monitor their actions and block activity that violates security rules.

That matters because an AI agent does not simply produce an answer and stop. It may access company files, connect to online services, run code or use other tools to complete a task. If it misinterprets an instruction or is manipulated, those permissions can create risks beyond a misleading chatbot response.

Nvidia’s approach puts security controls outside the AI agent itself, rather than relying on the agent to police its own behavior. Its reference architecture combines computing systems for running AI with BlueField-4 data processing units and Nvidia’s Sentry security framework to monitor activity and enforce restrictions.

Companies including Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO), CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD), Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Alphabet Inc‘s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Google Cloud are working with the architecture, Nvidia said.

Read Also: Amazon Challenges Nvidia's CUDA Moat With Trainium

The Potential Cost of Safety

In his note following GTC Berlin, Ackerman said OpenShell could slow runtime by as much as 25%. That is an analyst estimate, not a confirmed performance result across all tasks or deployments.

The potential trade-off is straightforward: More checks can mean more work before an AI agent is allowed to act. For businesses, the question is whether added safeguards justify any delay, particularly when agents are expected to handle time-sensitive work or perform thousands of tasks at once.

Still, a slower but controlled agent may be more useful to an enterprise than a faster system that can access information or take actions it should not. The actual balance will depend on the task, security settings and implementation.

What It Means for Nvidia

OpenShell reflects Nvidia’s effort to sell more than the chips that power AI. As companies move from testing AI assistants to giving them access to real business systems, security could become an increasingly important part of enterprise AI spending.

For investors, the key question is whether businesses adopt Nvidia’s approach at scale and whether its security controls can protect agents without materially hurting performance. Independent benchmarks and customer deployments will matter more than the launch announcement alone.

If Nvidia can make AI agents safer without making them meaningfully slower, security could become another reason businesses choose its broader platform.

The Nasdaq 100 rallied 1.2% on Monday as chipmakers rebounded and investors piled back into AI hardware.

Much of what we know about the stock market comes from a mix of theory and empirical evidence.

For example, the idea that earnings drive stock prices is supported by the view that a business’s value is tied to how much money it makes. And decades of market data show that stock prices and earnings have exhibited a tight correlation.

There are also ideas that make intuitive sense, but the evidence supporting them is shoddy. In the stock market, this is a big problem because people will trade on these ideas, only to underperform the market.

Especially when it comes to price behavior, if a theory were both sound and reliable, we’d probably hear more about people consistently beating the market with some bulletproof trading strategy. But we don’t.

With that in mind, here are five ideas about the stock market that I’d describe as myths or misunderstandings.

1. Stock market returns revert to a mean

Periods of strong stock market returns should be followed by periods of weak returns, and vice versa. Right?

If you take a long-term chart of the stock market and add a trendline, you’ll see prices above the line for some time and below it most of the time. This makes it tempting to say that the market exhibits mean reversion, or a tendency to gravitate back toward some historical average.

Unfortunately, this behavior is so inconsistent that Professors Paul Marsh, Mike Staunton, and Elroy Dimson concluded that "popular evidence for mean reversion is an ‘optical illusion’ that employs hindsight." They addressed this issue in the 2025 edition of UBS’s "Global Investment Returns Yearbook" and also explored it at length in the 2013 edition, when Credit Suisse published it.

They even went so far as to compare the belief in mean reversion to the Gambler’s Fallacy, the assumption that past outcomes inform future ones.

If mean reversion in the market were consistent and predictable, then there would be a way to trade the phenomenon in such a way as to generate above-average returns. But you don’t really hear about funds or traders consistently beating the market by trading the expectation of mean reversion. (Maybe some secretive hedge fund somewhere has figured it out and they’re not telling us.)

"Market-timing strategies based on mean reversion typically gave lower, not higher, returns," Marsh, Staunton, and Dimson found.

That’s not too surprising when you see the various stats showing periods of strong returns are often followed by more strong returns. Indeed, history shows that investing at all-time highs has produced better returns than investing on all other days.

Keep this in mind the next time someone suggests we’re "due" for weak returns because we just experienced strong returns. What just happened won’t tell you what’s coming next.

2. Valuations revert to a mean

One of the most popular ways to measure value is to divide an asset’s price by its earnings. This is the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. When a stock’s P/E is above its historical average, it’s considered expensive. When it’s below average, it’s considered cheap.

This has led many to assume that expensive stocks tend to get cheaper and cheap stocks tend to get more expensive. In other words, valuations tend to revert to a mean, right?

"We cannot emphasize enough that valuation metrics are NOT historically mean-reverting," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in January. They’ve characterized it as "an oft-repeated myth."

The firm has advanced this controversial view since 2013 (and again in 2022 and 2025). To make their point, they used a Dickey-Fuller test, a tool statisticians use to analyze time-series data. The test found that P/E ratios lacked stationarity, which means the averages aren’t stable over time.

This conclusion aligns with arguments from some top Wall Street strategists in recent years. They’ve argued that persistent improvements in business performance and capital structures have justified the higher valuations we’ve seen lately, an idea supported by theory.

And so, the mean itself is moving.

The idea that valuations aren’t mean-reverting probably makes a lot of people uncomfortable. Then again, trading based on the assumption of mean reversion hasn’t exactly yielded consistent results for people.

3. Picking a market-beating stock is like calling a coin flip

One of the main reasons to buy the stock of a single company is that you believe the price will outperform the market average over some period of time. Otherwise, you’d just put that money into an index fund tracking the market average.

A lot of people try their hand at stock picking. But most fail to beat the market.

Why? Because most stocks lag the market. And it’s far more than half.

In a study published last year, S&P Dow Jones Indices analysts found that just 19% of S&P 500 companies outperformed the average stock’s return from 2001 to 2025. Most S&P stocks underperformed the index in 13 of the past 24 calendar years.

Even with stock correlations very low and dispersion high — conditions that theoretically favor those looking to beat the market — professional stock pickers have struggled to identify winners!

The truth is that market averages, which have trended higher over the years, are driven by a relatively small number of stocks that generate eye-popping returns. ASU Professor Hendrik Bessembinder has published several studies showing this. Even Warren Buffett has attributed Berkshire Hathaway’s outstanding equity portfolio performance to "a few winners."

4. Holding a market-beating stock is a fun experience

Let’s say you got lucky and managed to buy one of these few stocks that go on to smoke the rest of the market. Buckle up.

In a report published last year, Morgan Stanley’s Michael Mauboussin and Dan Callahan studied the price behavior of 6,500 stocks. They took a closer look at the 20 stocks with the best total shareholder returns over the 40 years from 1985 to 2024.

"The median maximum drawdown was 72% for the best group, and the median maximum drawdown duration, the time from peak to trough, was 2.9 years," they found. "The median time to return to the prior peak was 4.3 years."

Just thinking about one of my positions losing 72% of its value makes me queasy, even knowing full well this is the average behavior of the best stocks.

If you’re a fund manager with picks like this, you may be fired long before you’ve been proven right.

5. The stock market often delivers average returns

The first thing many of us are taught about the stock market is that the average annual return is about 8% to 10%, give or take a point or two.

That gives many people the impression that the market climbs 8% to 10%-ish somewhat frequently.

But that’s far from the truth.

Carson Group’s Ryan Detrick ran the numbers. Since 1950, the S&P 500 returned 8%-10% in just four years.

In reality, the long-term average is the result of many above-average years and many below-average years. Ritholtz Wealth Management’s Ben Carlson observed that in the average up-year, the S&P returned 21%. And in the average down-year, the index lost 13%.

This doesn’t mean you should throw these ideas out the window

Maybe you’d be ill-advised to try to beat the market by trading on one of these myths or misunderstandings.

But that doesn’t mean you should ignore them entirely.

Sometimes, weak returns follow strong returns, valuations move toward the mean, half the stocks you pick beat the market, the outperforming stocks you own never lag, and we get an average year in the market.

In other words, sometimes we do get those brief moments when the market behaves as our gut expects.

Just because the markets can be chaotic and unpredictable doesn’t mean they never make sense. It’s just that they don’t make sense on a predictable schedule.
